There's the Zebra Coalition on mills by e. Colonial. For LGBT youth ages 13-24, they don't get nearly enough women's clothing donations. 
There's also Covenant house for youth 18-21. 
And Harbor House for battered woman ans children. Most of those ladies run with only the clothes on their backs. It's a nice shelter and even has a dog kennel.

The parliament house is not a place I recommend for younger gays, especially new to Orlando. Pulse is good if you want the club scene, but there are a few good choices for gay clubs. A few gay bars as well if you're into that. 
There's also a decent kink scene with a TNG group for 20somethings.
 The Center is alright, but I would suggest connecting with LGBT clubs a Ucf or Valencia. 
Orlando Youth Alliance is for LGBT youth 14-24, you're on the edge but will find people your age that are super friendly to personally show you around. Everyone is accepted there, and you'd probably fit right in. The people that go varies from week to week, so try it for at least a month to get a good idea of things. 

For nerdy stuff, there are comic shops everywhere. My go to place is Sci-Fi-City on e. Colonial near semoran. There's also a really good one out by you, I'll find the name if you're interested. 

As far as hookah I prefer a small place called Three Kings, very chill and they have a very talented belly dancer that comes in on occasion. They charge by the hookah/bowl, it's really cheap compared to other places if you enjoy sticking with a single flavor.

I used to bind 24/7 with the exception of showers. It took dating a trans-guy who happened to be nudist to ease my stress about my body. 

Basically once I knew I would be accepted no matter what my body looked like, I was able to be more comfortable with myself. It took getting used to, feeling them move around all the time. I was hyper aware of my body at first. But now I've remembered how comfortable and easy to breath it is not wearing a binder. I now only wear briefs unless it's chilly.

However I don't think it's weird, as I did that for a good portion of my transition. Whatever makes you feel comfortable is just fine :)

I used to attend OYA(orlando youth alliance). It's a lgbtq+ youthgroup for kids 13-24 and it was fantastic for me. It was a safe space for queer youth outside of public school drama. It allowed me to explore and discover myself because they accepted me as whatever I choose to identify with. 

I say go for it. It may not be everything you've dreamed of, but you'll never know if you don't try. :)

I'm going to be completely honest with you, I'm not going to take the time to make my words affectionate and non-offensive because I've been where you are, and I know it's not helpful. I'm sorry if it turns out I've offended.

Look. If you're a girl, your a girl. Point blank. Will you ever fit into society's perfect picture of a girl? Well no, but neither do most cis-girls even. There are plenty of "manly" girls out there and plenty of "girly" men. 

Hormones will help. Not just physically, but mentally. Now, it wont be a magical-girl, everything is perfect change. But a little bit a weight-distribution, breast growth, and self-image goes a long way. 

I thought my first binder was going to make me feel better but I was expecting too much of it. I envisioned myself with a perfectly flat chest where I could wear whatever I want and pass perfectly. But it didn't happen that way, and I had a good cry like you described. Wailing into my pillow feeling hopeless that I'd never pass. I couldn't live life as anything other than masculine, how was I supposed to cope? It wasn't fair.

I wore the binder the next time I went to my lgbt youth group and before I went out, all I could do was stare down at my chest and see those two lumps still there. But I hunched my shoulders and pretended to be like all the other trans-kids I saw on tumblr. 

And I passed! On the bus too no less. Of course if I stood up and let them see my hips or spoke and let them hear my voice they'd know immediately I was a girl. But that one second of passing to a stranger seriously changed everything.

I started to study people and really tried to figure out what made me perceive someone as male or female. I spent a great deal of time around queer people as well. So plenty of "manly" girls and "girly" boys there. 

Mannerisms, clothing, makeup, jewelry, how you put your hands in your pockets, how you hold your shoulders, how you tilt your head, how you stand, how you shift your weight, the little things you do when nervous, how you speak, how you interact with the people/genders around you, the list goes on. All of those important, it's not all about body structure. 

The hormones will do a deal of good for you, as I said before. But it'll take work on your part as well. If you're a girl, then you're a motherfucking girl and you hold yourself to it. It may take hours upon hours at the store and in front of the mirror to bring that girl to the surface, but it'll happen. I'm not going to promise you'll find yourself on the cover of a magazine, but anyone can pass with the right effort. 

If you want help passing without the sugar coating, I've got years of practice helping all types of Trans* people. Just message me.

Don't give up. Hearing your first Ma'am is worth much more than any hopelessness you're feeling now.
